title: The Berlin Airlift ends, 1949 — and the Candy Bomber, Gail Halvorsen
sources: Wikipedia: Berlin Blockade — Soviets blocked the Western Allies' railway, road and canal access to West Berlin (24 June 1948); only the air corridors had agreements and remained open; the Berlin Airlift ran from 26 June 1948 to 30 September 1949, officially ending on 30 September 1949 after fifteen months; American and British air forces carried food, fuel (nearly two-thirds of the tonnage was coal) and other necessities; at the height of the airlift, one plane reached West Berlin every thirty seconds; Operation Little Vittles, candy-dropping 'raisin bombers'

Wikipedia: Gail Halvorsen — C-54 pilot on the airlift; in July 1948 met about thirty children at the barbed-wire fence at Tempelhof; gave them his two sticks of gum; they broke them into pieces and those without sniffed the wrappers; promised to drop more from his plane and to wiggle his wings so they would know it was him; made parachutes out of handkerchiefs for the candy rations; nicknamed 'Uncle Wiggly Wings'; Operation Little Vittles dropped over 23 tons of candy; many of those pilots had previously taken part in WWII operations against German cities

Archive film: 'Berlin airlift' — British Central Office of Information film, Wikimedia Commons, public domain (low pass over a Berlin S-Bahn station, landings, bread in a West Berlin bakery, coal unloading, a Berlin boy, crowds at an airlift plane)

Photos (public domain, USAF / US Army / USDA via Wikimedia Commons): Halvorsen and crew rigging candy parachutes; a C-54 making a Little Vittles candy drop; Berliners watching a C-54 land at Tempelhof, 1948 (Henry Ries); Berlin youngsters near Tempelhof, 1948; official portrait of Stalin, 1940s

post.facebook:
On this day in 1949, the Berlin Airlift came to an end.

In June 1948, Stalin had blocked every road, railway and canal into West Berlin. Only the air corridors stayed open — so American and British planes flew in food, fuel and, above all, coal. At the height of the airlift, a plane reached the city every thirty seconds.

One of the pilots, Gail Halvorsen, met about thirty children at the fence of Tempelhof airport. He had only two sticks of gum. The children broke them into pieces and shared them; the ones who got none sniffed the wrappers.

He promised to drop more from his plane — and to wiggle his wings so they would know it was him. He tied candy to parachutes made from handkerchiefs. Other pilots joined in, and more than 23 tons of candy fell on Berlin.

A few years earlier, many of these pilots had flown against German cities. Now Berlin's children called one of them Uncle Wiggly Wings.
